examples: Grandpa got sick so I am worried.
이 병은 약으로 고칠 수 있어요.
This illness can be cured with medicine.
I caught a serious disease so I was hospitalized.
nuance: For getting sick Koreans say 병이 나다 with 나다, the same verb used for fever. To catch a disease use 병에 걸리다 with the particle 에, just like 감기에 걸리다.
mistakes: Saying 병을 걸리다 instead of 병에 걸리다

examples: I got a shot at the hospital.
The child is scared of shots.
The nurse gives a shot in the arm.
nuance: To receive a shot Koreans say 주사를 맞다 with 맞다, which literally means to be hit. The nurse giving the shot uses 주사를 놓다, so the verb depends on who acts.
mistakes: Saying 주사를 받다 instead of 주사를 맞다

examples: I am getting treatment at the hospital.
The treatment is over so now I am fine.
nuance: To receive treatment Koreans say 치료를 받다 with 받다, meaning to receive. The verb 치료하다 means to treat someone, so a patient uses 받다 while a doctor uses 하다.
mistakes: Saying 치료를 맞다 instead of 치료를 받다

examples: There are many patients at the hospital today.
nuance: For a doctor examining someone Koreans say 환자를 보다 with 보다, meaning to look at. Beginners often use 만나다 for meet, but a medical visit always uses 보다 here.
mistakes: Saying 환자를 만나요 for a doctor examining a patient

examples: I check the body temperature with a thermometer.
The baby body temperature is too high.
The temperature is normal so it is a relief.
nuance: To measure temperature Koreans say 체온을 재다 with 재다, the same verb used for height and length. Saying 체온을 보다 sounds odd because temperature is measured, not looked at.
mistakes: Saying 체온을 봐요 instead of 체온을 재요

examples: I check my blood pressure at the hospital.
My father has high blood pressure.
My blood pressure is low so I feel dizzy.
nuance: Like body temperature, blood pressure is measured with 재다, so Koreans say 혈압을 재다. For high or low pressure use 높다 and 낮다, not 크다 or 작다 which mean big and small.
mistakes: Saying 혈압이 커요 instead of 혈압이 높아요

examples: I fell and got a wound on my knee.
The wound is deep so I go to the hospital.
I applied medicine so the wound healed.
nuance: For getting a wound Koreans say 상처가 나다 with 나다, the same verb used for fever and illness. When a wound heals use 낫다, which also means to recover from sickness.
mistakes: Saying 상처를 받다 for a physical wound, which means emotional hurt

examples: I have a cough because of a cold.
I cough a lot at night.
I took medicine so the cough stopped.
nuance: Koreans say both 기침이 나다 and 기침을 하다 for coughing, and both sound natural. The form 기침이 나다 uses 나다 like fever and runny nose, treating symptoms as something that comes out.
mistakes: Saying 기침을 가지다 instead of 기침이 나요

usage: there is a lot of snot
examples: I caught a cold so I have a runny nose.
I wipe the snot with a tissue.
After taking medicine the runny nose stopped.
nuance: For a runny nose Koreans say 콧물이 나다 with 나다, the verb for symptoms that come out. This is the natural way to describe a cold, unlike saying 코가 아프다 which means real nose pain.
mistakes: Saying 코가 아파요 to mean a runny nose

examples: I have had a headache since morning.
The headache was so bad that I lay down.
I take headache medicine and rest a bit.
nuance: 두통 is the formal word for headache, while 머리가 아프다 is the everyday spoken form. Both are correct, but Koreans often just say 머리가 아파요 in daily talk and save 두통 for the pharmacy.
mistakes: Saying 두통이 아파요, since 두통 already means the pain

examples: I ate too much so I have indigestion.
If you eat slowly digestion goes well.
nuance: For digestion Koreans use 소화가 되다 with 되다, so 소화가 안 되다 means indigestion. Saying 소화를 하다 sounds unnatural because digestion happens to you rather than being something you do.
mistakes: Saying 소화를 못 해요 instead of 소화가 안 돼요

examples: My health has improved a lot lately.
I exercise to take care of my health.
Happy new year and stay healthy.
nuance: 건강하세요 is a warm everyday farewell meaning stay healthy, used like a blessing. As an adjective 건강하다 means to be healthy, so you can say 저는 건강해요 to mean I am healthy.
mistakes: Saying 건강이 높아요 instead of 건강이 좋아요
